BEAM subtlety the untimed model hides: any message resets a GenServer timeout, including :sys.get_state polls. The driver never saw the timeout until it stopped polling. In the model a timeout may fire regardless, which is the safe direction
nodes.description: Untimed timers over-approximate: the model admits a timeout firing after a pong. The real system under-fires when the mailbox is busy. Safety proofs hold in both; liveness of the watchdog (a hung worker is eventually replaced) would need the timer to actually fire, i.e. a fairness assumption on timers plus quiet mailboxes.

Defer clause and loop_tail semantics: a loop module with no unguarded bare-pattern clause gets '| me, _, .<mod> s_0.., m => (.<mod> s_0.., [.send me m])' after its last clause; tail 'f(e)' -> {:noreply, e}, 'exit(r)' kept, statement kept then exit(:normal), plain value -> exit(:normal); rewriting descends through if/case

Why it matters: this is the encoding of selective receive; the re-enqueue delivers to self, so the message count of the process is preserved and the proof must frame it (mcount_deliver). The explorer never sends start/EXIT to a worker, so the defer clause does not enlarge the explored state space; it is exercised by beh_eq_gen and the SupervisorProof cases, not by the checker.

nodes.description: NOTES section 6, replace the bullet "Exit reasons collapse to normal | error ... under-approximation" with: "Exit reasons are normal, error and kill. Process.exit(p, :kill) is the untrappable kill it is on the BEAM: the target dies whatever it traps and its links and monitors see error (:killed). A remote Process.exit(p, :normal) is ignored by a non-trapping target and is an EXIT message to a trapping one. nodes.title: Semantics of the generation encoding and its remaining approximations
nodes.description: Exact w.r.t. the BEAM for processed messages: a receive entry arms exactly one live timer (generation = state gen) and any message handled by an arm cancels it by moving to gen+1, so a stale after_<loop> (carried gen != state gen) is consumed and ignored (`stale_ignored` in TtlProof). Two things remain approximations, both towards more behaviours: (1) timers are still untimed, so the live timer may fire before or after any message; (2) the defer clause and a failed guard re-enter at gen+1 and arm a fresh timer, whereas the BEAM keeps the original timeout running when it skips a non-matching message (the model can delay the expiry across skipped messages; it cannot produce an expiry the BEAM could not, because the fresh timer may fire immediately). The old accumulation approximation (a stale after firing late after other messages were handled) is gone. Lean has no non-linear patterns, so the stale-ignore is the else branch of the after clause (`| me, _, .cache v gen, .after_run gen' => if gen' = gen then ... else (.cache v gen, [])`), placed before the defer clause; it is not a separate Lean clause. Timers still accumulate in Sys.timers (stale entries stay until fired); no timer-cancel effect was added to Sys.lean. Checker counts: explore beh sig init 7 3 = 16,723 (was 17,206), mutant behNoRaise caught after 29 configurations: timer 0, run 0, timer 0, run 0, env put 0 -> 0, run 0 (two live expiries then put 0). Stage A ranks the pending (0, c, _) signal by its position in the FIFO queue (a run only appends signals, a signal step pops the head), stage B ranks EXIT c _ by its position in the supervisor mailbox (every other step only appends to it, run 0 pops the head and either spawns or leaves the state alone). README, a new paragraph (suggested under the generic-explorer paragraph, title **Differential testing.**): 'The interpreters `run` and `runSys` are also tested against the BEAM. `Leanactors/Replay.lean` is an executable that replays a script of scheduler choices (environment deliveries, actor runs, signal/DOWN/timer firings) on one example and prints the observable part of the final configuration; `elixir/fuzz.exs` generates such scripts at random and drives the same messages into the real modules. The BEAM has its own scheduler, so scripts are built from phases that have a single outcome under any scheduling (one target per phase; the twin waits for the phase to end via `:sys.get_state` queued behind the message, a receive trace, or a DOWN): bank casts, ticks and audits including a tick deferred during a blocking call; ttl puts, asks, the live timer expiring (a real 300ms sleep) and `put 0` killing the cache, with stale-timer firings replayed in Lean only since the BEAM cancelled them; lock ticks expanded through a simulation of the protocol including the grant cascade and one deferred tick per waiting client. Observables: bank balance, each client's last seen value and pending messages; the cache's value, the reader's count, every value the reader received and pending; the lock's holder and queue, each client's phase and pending. Where the two sides legitimately differ (untimed timers, real time, scheduling), the generator is constrained rather than the comparison. Mutants of the BEAM modules (a withdraw off by one, a get ignored, LIFO grant) are caught within the first runs.'
NOTES section 10 (Round 5) bullet: 'Differential fuzzing (node 442): a `replay` executable over `run`/`runSys` and `elixir/fuzz.exs`. The interesting design point is that the BEAM cannot be told which process to run next, so a script is only comparable if every phase has one outcome under any scheduling; the fuzzer's header documents each phase shape and why. Two things surfaced while building it: the ttl comparison must treat stale timers as Lean-only (the model over-approximates the BEAM's cancelled timeouts, as section 6 says) and treat a stalled driver as a possible spurious expiry (retried, counted); and a lock client blocked in a call cannot answer a system message, so its phase is read off the server's queue. The fuzzer is checked for sensitivity with BEAM mutants (not committed): withdraw n<b, get ignored for one value, LIFO grant, each caught in the first runs.'

## Readiness

`elixir elixir/readiness.exs PATH...` answers 'what would it take to translate this file?' for any Elixir source, where PATH is a .ex file or a directory. For every module that uses `GenServer` or contains a `receive` it runs the translator with its output discarded (retrying with `--pid` when the only complaint is an unregistered send target, which is configuration rather than a construct) and, independently, walks the module's AST against `@supported`, an allowlist at the top of the harness that mirrors the header of `elixir/to_lean.exs`. The walk is what makes the report complete: the translator stops at its first error, the walker reports every unsupported construct with its file, line and a stable kind (`Map.pop/2`, `try/rescue`, `defstruct`, `Phoenix.PubSub.broadcast/3`, `no @type state (untyped mode not available)`, `field access s.field`). Findings are blockers or notes -- a note is something the translator ignores silently, or that only needs a flag. `--markdown` renders the report as `docs/readiness.md`, `--strict` exits non-zero if any candidate module is not translatable, and `check.sh` uses that over `elixir/src` so a translator change that narrows the subset is caught.

`docs/readiness.md` is that report over the lib trees of five real applications: 373 files, 55 GenServer or receive-loop modules, none of them translatable today, 2838 blocking constructs grouped both by kind and by the translator feature each group would need. The round is planned from that table rather than from guesses.

README new paragraph **Untyped mode** (text): A module that declares no @type has its declarations inferred from its own source before anything else runs, so every decision downstream is still type-directed. Message unions come from the handle_cast/handle_info/handle_call clause patterns (a tag at the arity it is matched with, the callback fixing the kind) and from the literal messages the module sends that nobody handles; the reply type from every {:reply, r, _} in the file when all are literal atoms or tagged tuples (a tag at two arities, :ok and {:ok, ref}, names the tuple form ok1); the state from the literal of init/1, where a map with atom keys is a record. Every inferred field is term(), rendered as the opaque Term of Leanactors/Term.lean, which carries a number and nothing else: enough for DecidableEq, which every map key needs, and for fresh references. A @type declaration, where there is one, refines those fields exactly as before, which is what gradual typing means here; the seven annotated sources translate byte for byte.
README new paragraph **Record-shaped state**: a @type state or an init literal %{k: e, ..} with atom keys becomes one St constructor with NAMED fields. A whole-state variable binds the fields the body reads (state.f is the field, %{state | f: e} rebuilds the constructor with that field replaced, a bare state is the whole constructor) and the others are _; a map pattern %{f: p, ..} = state binds the named fields to their sub-patterns. README new paragraph **External resources**: :ets.new(..) on the right of a binding is a fresh opaque reference. nodes.title: Translator limits and rules found by the log store shape
nodes.description: 1) A struct-shaped state is flattened, so no value of that struct type ever exists in the model; binding one (s2 = %(state | f: v) then returning s2) is refused with a clear message. The state must be returned directly, or its fields bound. 2) hd/1 raises on the BEAM but an expression here cannot, so it renders as List.headD at the element type's default; an element type with no default (a tagged union) is an error that asks you to match on the list instead. 3) A capture is one-argument only (&1); &2 has nothing to refer to. 4) x1 is reserved as the binder of a capture. 5) Enum.map's result element type is inferred from the lambda body when possible, otherwise an expected type is needed. 6) A statement with an effect (a send, a spawn) before an if/case body is refused: it would have to be pushed into every branch. 7) An .exs driver cannot use struct literals, because a script is expanded before Code.require_file has run; struct/2 is the workaround, and elixir/ringlog.exs says so. 8) Declarations must be emitted in dependency order (a struct used by a tagged union first): Lean has no forward references. 9) A whole-state part the right-hand side never mentions must be renamed _part or Lean's unused-variable linter warns.

README, a new paragraph after the Maps paragraph:

Structs. `defstruct f: d, ..` with `@type t :: %__MODULE__{f: T, ..}` becomes a Lean `structure` whose fields carry the defstruct defaults, so `%Mod{f: e}` is `({ f := e } : Mod)`, `x.f` is the projection and `%Mod{f: p}` a pattern on the anonymous constructor. When a GenServer's `@type state` is its own struct -- the shape of a real Phoenix `LogStore` -- the struct is flattened into that module's state constructor, one Lean field per defstruct field: `state.f` is the part the clause's pattern bound to f and `%{state | f: e}` rebuilds the constructor with the named parts replaced. Nothing else in the translator changes, which is the point of the flattening: field coverage, crash clauses, the whole-state alias and the hidden `gen` field of a receive loop all keep working. Enum over lists is the List API (filter/map/reject/count/any?/all?/member?/reverse/take/drop/at/empty?, `length`, `hd`/`tl`, `++` and the comprehension `for x <- l, c, do: e`), with `fn x -> e end` and the capture `&(&1.f == v)` as Lean lambdas; `hd` is `List.headD` at the element type's default, because it raises on the BEAM and an expression in the model cannot. An Erlang queue is the list, oldest first: `:queue.in` appends, `{_, q} = :queue.out(q0)` is `let q := List.tail q0`, `:queue.to_list` is the identity and `case :queue.out(q)` matches head and rest at once.

NOTES round-6 bullet for this piece:

structs, Enum and :queue (node 561). The target was `Ensemble.LogStore`, a ring buffer whose state is its own struct. Two shapes were on the table (567, 569): keep the state as one Lean field of a `structure`, or flatten the struct into the state constructor. Flattening won (570) because everything the translator already does to a multi-field state -- coverage of the fields, the crash clauses, the whole-state alias a fallthrough needs, the hidden generation field of a receive loop -- keeps working unchanged, and the Gen files stay in the shape the proofs read. The cost is that a value of the state's struct type never exists in the model, so binding one is a translator error with a message saying to return the state or bind its fields. Three things surprised (610): Lean has no forward references, so declarations had to be emitted in dependency order once a struct could appear inside a tagged union; a whole-state part the body never mentions trips the unused-variable linter, so it is renamed `_part`; and an .exs driver cannot write `%Entry{}` at all, because a script is expanded before its `Code.require_file` has run. The ringlog invariant (count is the queue's length, and at most the cap) is proved the cheap way: `ok_step` says one behaviour step preserves it, `beh_no_spawn` says the behaviour emits no spawning effect, and `SysStep.stateOf_spawn_cases` from SysProps turns those two into `count_invariant` over every configuration reachable under unbounded scheduling. nodes.title: Integrator record for wf7/locals: README/NOTES replacement text
nodes.description:
No README.md or NOTES.md edit was made on wf7/locals, per the round rules. Proposed text for the integrator, to be merged with the other branches' numbers.

README, in the "Supported subset" list (a new bullet after the init/1 bullet):

  - **Module-local functions.** A `def`/`defp` that is not a callback and
    that a callback reaches, directly or through another helper, becomes a
    Lean definition emitted before `beh`, named `<module>_<function>`; a call
    to it renders as a call. Its body must be in the pure fragment: `if`,
    `cond` and `case` as expressions, a block of bindings ending in a value,
    and everything the expression translator already renders. A helper that
    sends, spawns or logs has no effect the model could carry, so it is an
    error naming the helper -- once, not once per call site. Argument and
    result types come from a `@spec` when the module gives one and otherwise
    from the types the helper is called at. A helper that recurses on the
    tail of a list argument is an ordinary `def`; any other self-recursion
    takes a leading `fuel : Nat` and is called with the constant `localFuel`,
    which the generated file documents as an approximation. Mutual recursion
    is an error naming both helpers.

README, amending the init/1 bullet:

    `init/1` may now be a block: `Process.flag(:trap_exit, true)`, a PubSub
    subscribe, a `Logger` call (dropped), a call to a local helper, and
    bindings `v = e` of pure expressions, which are substituted into the
    state expression -- `init/1` has no Lean binder of its own, because the
    state is built at the spawn site. The option list a real `init/1` is
    handed is not modelled: a parameter used as one is the empty keyword
    list, so `Keyword.get(opts, :k, d)` is its literal default and the
    translator warns.

README, amending the untyped-mode paragraph:

    A module with no `@type state` and no `init/1` to infer one from now
    reads the shape off its callbacks' state patterns: a map pattern anywhere
    makes it a record whose fields are the keys the patterns match and the
    keys the bodies update or return, tuple patterns of one size make it
    positional, and patterns that only bind the state whole leave it the
    opaque `Term`.

README, Readiness section, numbers to fold in (wf7/locals alone, over the
five projects): blockers 1621 -> 1510; the family `call to a helper in the
same module` (271 occurrences in 41 modules, the largest) is replaced by
`local helper is not a pure expression` (254 in 40), which names a function
instead of a call site; `statement in init/1` 89/26 -> 21/15; `no @type state
and no init/1 to infer one from` 24/24 -> 5/5. Translatable modules stay 1.

NOTES, a paragraph for the round-7 section:

    The biggest single family in the readiness report was never the actor
    model: it was 271 calls to helpers in the same module. Translating them
    turned out to be a question about *where the error goes*. Inlining the
    helper at each call site would have reported the same defect 271 times;
    emitting each helper as its own Lean definition reports it once, at the
    definition, and says what stops it. That is the difference between a
    symptom list and a work list, and it is why the new family count (254) is
    barely lower than the old one (271) while the report is far more useful.
    The second lesson was about types. A helper has no declared type in
    Elixir, so its Lean signature has to come from somewhere: a `@spec` when
    there is one, and otherwise the types it is *called* at. Inferring from
    use needs the call sites rendered, and rendering them needs the
    signatures, so the translator renders everything three times -- the first
    round sees only the callbacks, the next two see the helpers calling each
    other at the types they now have -- and lets the definition fix its own
    result type before any use does, so one opaque call site cannot make a
    typed helper opaque.

nodes.title: Translator limits found while building local functions
nodes.description:
Things found while building the local-function facility that a sibling or the integrator will hit.

1) A tagged union with exactly one alternative is not recognised. A file whose only reply literal is {:size, n} infers @type reply :: {:size, term()}, and lean_type/3 then fails with "unsupported type {:size, term()}" because a bare tuple type is only allowed at state level. Two alternatives work. This is pre-existing (untyped mode, infer_types/2), not something this branch introduced; worth a fix in the union-building code, which this branch does not own.

2) An unused `fresh` binder trips Lean's linter. A clause whose only spawn binds its pid to an unused variable ("{:ok, _p} = GenServer.start_link(..)") still renders the second beh binder as `fresh`, and Lean reports "Variable name `fresh` is not explicitly referenced" -- a warning, so check.sh fails. fresh_name/1 keys off :__fresh__ being in the env rather than off the pid actually being used. Worked around in the init_stmts fixture by using the pid.

3) A local binding whose right-hand side type is unknown gets no env entry. In a helper body, "let x := ..." with an untypable right-hand side leaves x untyped, so a later use of x at a typed position renders without the conversion. It does not misrender today (Lean infers the let), but a case scrutinee over such an x fails with "untyped scrutinee".

4) `[k | l]` is not an expression form. List cons is supported in patterns but not in expressions, so a handler that prepends has to write "l ++ [k]". Cheap to add, in the expression builder's area.

5) Elixir parses "def foo do .. end" with args = nil, not []. Both local_defs/2 in the translator and in the harness normalise with "args || []" so a zero-arity helper is found; a bare "foo" without parentheses is still a variable reference as far as the AST goes and is not rewritten to a call.

6) A pipe hides a local call's arity. "socket |> reload_prs()" is the node reload_prs/0, so the harness labels it an imported/macro call even though reload_prs/1 is defined in the module. That is why the "call to an imported function or macro" family barely moved (156 -> 155): most of it is genuine Phoenix imports (assign/2 and assign/3 are 123 of the 155), and the rest is this pipe artefact, which the pipe feature will absorb.

nodes.description:
README, the to_lean.exs row of the Layout table, replace with:
| `elixir/to_lean.exs` | The translator: `@type`-directed (`msg`, `cast`, `info`, `call`, `reply`, `state`), small subset, unverified; `handle_continue` is inlined, not sent; the pure fragment is compiled as a language, so any sub-expression may be an `if`, a `case`, a block or a binding (pipes, `cond` and `unless` are desugared away first) |

README, a new paragraph for the Readiness section (numbers are wf7/control alone, to be re-counted after the round is integrated):
Round 7 made the pure fragment a language rather than a body shape. An
expression may now be an `if`/`case`/`cond`, a block `(a; b; c)` (nested
`let`s) or a binding, `a |> f(b)` is rewritten to `f(a, b)` before anything
else looks at the module, and the Kernel type tests are decided statically
from the modelled type (`is_pid` on a `pid()` is `true`; an opaque `term()`
or a tagged union is an error, not a guess). A statement with an effect
before an `if`/`case` body is pushed into every branch instead of being
refused. Over the five real projects that took the blocker count from 1621
to 1421 and emptied eleven families outright, among them `if/case not at
body level` (98 occurrences in 28 modules), `pipe |>` (38) and `block as a
sub-expression` (26).

NOTES.md, a paragraph for the round-7 section:
The interesting constraint was totality. Lean's `let` has nothing to fall
through to, so a pattern binding is accepted only when the pattern is total
at its type -- a variable, `_`, a pair at a product type, a struct pattern
-- and `{:ok, v} = Map.fetch(m, k)` is a clear error telling you to match
instead. A `cond` must end in `true ->`, because falling off the end raises
CondClauseError and an expression in the model cannot raise. An `if` with
no `else` is nil, which the model has only at an Option type. The Kernel
type tests fall out of the same discipline from the other side: a value of
the model has exactly one type, so the test is a compile-time constant, and
where it is not (an opaque `Term`, a tagged union with both atom and tuple
alternatives, any binary) the translator says so rather than guessing.

nodes.title: cross-area edit: resource_noop?/2, hide_unused_parts/3, pat/5 atom+string clauses, expr/3 operator clause, type_of/2 field clause
nodes.description:
Five edits outside 'values and remote calls' that the integrator should expect in the merge of wf7/stdlib.

1. strip_resource_noops/resource_noop? (elixir/to_lean.exs, 'external resources' section). Added one clause:
     defp resource_noop?(_mod, e) when is_tuple(e) and tuple_size(e) == 3, do: remote_noop?(e)
   placed immediately before the existing catch-all. This is how every Logger call disappears (the @remote :noop rows), including inside init/1, and it is why a Logger argument never has to be translated. Keep both clauses in that order.

2. hide_unused_parts/3 (render_clauses). It used to hide only the parts of a __whole__ state variable; it now also hides any other pattern variable of the state that the rendered right-hand side does not mention. Needed because a clause whose only use of its state variable was a dropped Logger call would otherwise trip Lean's unused-variable linter, which check.sh treats as a failure. The '_'-prefix test moved from the comprehension into the reduce. No existing output changed (ten Gen files and 49 expectations byte-identical).

3. pat/5. Two changes: a new clause for a binary pattern (a Lean string literal pattern, rejected at a non-String position), and the atom clause now renders an atom at type Atom through atom_ctor/1 (which registers the key in the file's Atom inductive) before falling back to the enum reading. enum_type?/1 also excludes "String" so a string literal pattern never counts towards coverage.

4. expr/3, the binary-operator clause. It now fails with a message when either operand has type Instant and the operator is one of + - < > <= >=: the model has no clock, and the refusal should name that rather than surface as a missing Lean instance.

5. type_of/2 for . The struct branch used to return nil when the variable is not a struct; it now falls back to var_type/2, which knows the type of a record-state field. This is what makes  usable as a case scrutinee on a record state. Strictly a widening: it only turns nil into a type.

nodes.title: generic Lean helpers added by wf7/stdlib: Leanactors/Str.lean, Leanactors/SetList.lean, Leanactors/Time.lean
nodes.description:
Three new library files under Leanactors/, each announced here so no sibling duplicates them. All three are imported by Leanactors.lean and by a generated file only when it needs them (the translator decides from the rendered clauses, not only from the types).

Leanactors/Str.lean -- binaries.
  class ToStr (a : Type) where toStr : a -> String
  instances: String (identity), Nat, Int, Bool (toString), and a low-priority instance for any [Repr a].
  Str.toStr : the function the translator emits for an interpolation.
  Lemmas: toStr_string, toStr_nat, toStr_bool (all simp, all rfl), append_assoc, append_empty, empty_append (simp; they are String.append_assoc / append_empty / empty_append, which in Lean 4.33 take no explicit arguments).
  The low-priority Repr instance is the honest part: a value with no printable model still becomes some string, and it is Lean's repr, not the BEAM's to_string. A property may compare two interpolated strings, but must not depend on their bytes.

Leanactors/SetList.lean -- MapSet as a duplicate-free list in insertion order.
  contains, insert, erase, size, toList, ofList, union, difference, intersection, all over [DecidableEq a].
  Lemmas: contains_eq_mem, contains_nil, mem_insert, mem_insert_self, mem_of_mem_insert, insert_of_mem, not_mem_erase, mem_erase, size_nil, size_insert_of_mem, size_insert_of_not_mem, toList_eq, mem_difference, mem_intersection.
  Like AssocList it assumes nothing about its argument: the lemmas hold for any list, and insert is what keeps a set built from the empty list duplicate-free. toList is the identity, so it is in insertion order and not the BEAM's term order -- the one place this model is coarser than MapSet.

Leanactors/Time.lean -- the clock the model does not have.
  inductive Instant where now, deriving Repr, DecidableEq. No LT, no LE, no arithmetic, no ToString of its own.
  Lemmas: Instant.eq_now, Instant.all_eq (deliberately NOT simp: eq_now has a variable head and Lean warns).
  Two reads of the clock are equal because there is only one Instant. That is a fact about the model, not about time, and the doc comment says so; the translator refuses an order or an arithmetic on an Instant before Lean ever sees it.

If a sibling needs a string, a set or an instant in a hand-written example, use these, not a local copy.

nodes.title: translator bug (not fixed): the :all sentinel of covered_tags collides with a message tag named :all
nodes.description:
Found while writing the mapset fixture, NOT fixed (it is outside this branch's area and it fails loudly, so it is not a soundness hole).

covered_tags/3 returns a list of message tags and prepends the ATOM :all as a sentinel meaning "the bare-message clauses alone cover every state". insert_crashes/2 then asks `:all in total`. A module that declares a message tag literally named :all -- for instance @type call :: ... | :all, which is an ordinary name for "give me everything" -- makes that test true for the wrong reason. The module is then recorded as exhaustive, the global catch-all clause is suppressed, and Lean rejects the generated file with "Missing cases: ... Msg.reply ...".

Reproduce: any GenServer whose message union contains :all and whose @type reply produces an unhandled `reply` constructor. The mapset fixture had exactly that before its call was renamed from :all to :list.

The failure is always at Lean compile time, never a silently ignored message, so nothing proved is wrong. The fix is to stop using an atom that a source file can also use: have covered_tags return {tags, all_bare?} (or use a tuple sentinel), and change the two `:all in ...` tests in insert_crashes and covered_tags accordingly. Three call sites.

nodes.title: Integrator record for wf7/stdlib: README and NOTES replacement text, files touched, readiness delta
nodes.description:
Replacement text for the integrator (README.md and NOTES.md are not edited on this branch). Numbers are wf7/stdlib's contribution alone and must be re-counted after the round-7 merge.

--- README.md, new paragraph for the pipeline section (after the Maps / Enum / queue paragraphs) ---

Values. Elixir binaries are Lean `String`s: a `String.t()` or `binary()` in a
`@type`, a string literal, `<>` as `++`, a string literal in a pattern, and an
interpolation `"a#{e}b"` as `"a" ++ Str.toStr e ++ "b"`. `Str.toStr` is the
`ToStr` class of `Leanactors/Str.lean`; its instances for `String`, `Nat`,
`Int` and `Bool` are the BEAM's own rendering and everything else goes through
its derived `Repr`, which is deterministic but is not what `to_string` would
print, so no property should depend on the bytes of an interpolated string.
A keyword list is the association list `List (Atom x V)` over an `Atom`
inductive the generated file builds from the keys used, so `Keyword.*`,
`Access.get/2` and `opts[:k]` are the same `AssocList` a map is. A `MapSet` is
a duplicate-free list in insertion order (`Leanactors/SetList.lean`); its
`to_list` is in that order and not the BEAM's term order, the one place the
model is coarser than `MapSet`. A module name used as a value becomes a
constant of a generated `Module` inductive, so it can be stored, sent and
compared. And time is not modelled at all: `DateTime.utc_now/0`,
`System.monotonic_time/1` and their neighbours are the single opaque
`Instant.now` of `Leanactors/Time.lean`, which has equality and nothing else --
ordering or subtracting two instants is refused by the translator with a
message saying the model has no clock, rather than modelled wrongly. Logging is
not an effect: every `Logger` call is dropped, arguments included, before
anything is translated.

Standard-library calls are one table. `@remote` at the top of
`elixir/to_lean.exs` maps a module, function and arity to what the call becomes
-- a rendering, `:noop` (dropped) or `{:error, why}` (refused, with the reason).
Teaching the translator another standard-library function is adding a row.

--- NOTES.md, section 11 (round 7), the wf7/stdlib part ---

What blocked real code after round 6 was not actor semantics -- those were
done -- but ordinary functional Elixir, and the largest single group was
values. 147 string literals in 25 modules, 85 interpolations in 18, 67 keyword
lists in 12, 40 Logger calls in 15, 37 Keyword and 24 Access lookups, 17 clock
reads, 11 MapSets, 11 module names used as values.

The design question each family asks is the same: what is the honest Lean
model, and where does it stop? Binaries were easy (Lean's `String` has
`DecidableEq` and `Repr`, which is everything a state field needs) except for
interpolation, which has to render values the model knows nothing about. The
answer is a `ToStr` class with faithful instances for the four types whose
Elixir rendering is known and a low-priority instance through `Repr` for
everything else -- so the translation never fails for want of a rendering, and
the doc comment says plainly which strings are artefacts.

Time was the family where the honest answer was "no". A clock read could have
been a fresh opaque value from a hidden counter, the way `:ets.new` is; but
clock reads appear deep inside expressions (`%{status: "running", started_at:
DateTime.utc_now()}`), not on the right of a binding, so threading a counter
through the expression renderer would have been real machinery in exchange for
a model still too weak to prove anything about elapsed time. Instead there is
exactly one `Instant`, every read returns it, and `<`, `>`, `+`, `-` and
`DateTime.diff` are translation errors that name the reason. A module whose
behaviour depends on time passing is not translated with its timing quietly
wrong; it is rejected.

Logging turned out to be the cheapest large win. A `Logger.info("x #{y}")` is
three blockers -- a call, a string, an interpolation -- and none of them has to
be supported, because the call is dropped before translation with its arguments
untranslated. Dropping it in `strip_resource_noops`, next to the `:ets`
statements, put it in `init/1` and in every callback at once. The one
consequence worth knowing: a pattern variable whose only use was the log line
becomes unused, so `hide_unused_parts` now hides any unused state variable and
not only the parts of a whole-state one.

The lasting piece is the shape rather than any one family: one `@remote` table
of {module, function, arity} to a rendering, `:noop` or `{:error, why}`, with
four rendering kinds (an association-list operation, a `SetList` function, a
constant, a Lean function at given types). The next round extends the subset by
adding rows.

Over the five real projects the blocker count fell from 1621 to 1164 and every
one of these families left the planning table. No module crossed into
"translated" on this branch alone: the modules that are closest are held up by
local helper calls, statements in `init/1` and nested `if`/`case`, which are
the other two builders' areas.

nodes.title: LiveView constructs left unsupported on purpose
nodes.description:
Constructs I decided NOT to support this round, each with the reason.
1. assign_new/3 and update/3 (the other LiveView assigns helpers). assign_new takes a zero-argument fn whose value is only computed when the key is absent -- in the model a record field is always present, so assign_new is always the no-op branch, which is true of a mounted socket but not of one being mounted. Since the lifecycle is not modelled at all, emitting the no-op would be asserting something about mount that the model cannot see. Left blocked.
2. assign with a computed key (assign(socket, key, v) where key is a variable). The state is a record with a fixed set of fields; a computed key needs a real map, which the socket is not here. Left as the unsupported call it is, with a fixture pinning the error.
3. Rebinding the socket inside a callback body (socket = assign(socket, ...), then using it). The whole-state variable has no type in the model to give the let, so the binding fails. A LiveView often writes this; LogsLive does not, so I left it.
4. A Reply inductive for the mixed reply case (see node 722).

nodes.title: Sentinel collision: a module with a :all message tag defeated the coverage check
nodes.description: The LiveView fixture found a latent bug that had nothing to do with LiveView. covered_tags/3 returns the list of message tags a module covers exhaustively, and prepended the atom :all as a sentinel meaning "the bare-message clauses cover every state". A module with a message tag literally named :all therefore looked fully covered: insert_crashes would emit no crash clause for its uncovered cast/call tags and no global catch-all, and Lean would reject the generated file with a missing-cases error (or, worse for a cast tag, the model would silently not crash where the BEAM would). The sentinel is :__every__ now, which no Elixir atom tag can be. Found because my first draft of the reply fixture used handle_call(:all, ...) for "give me everything".

nodes.description:
The brief asked for a general cross-module mechanism. I chose the sound one (resolve the callee's own def and translate it exactly like a local helper: same inlining, same pure-fragment rule, just across a module boundary in the same compilation unit) and then MEASURED what it would buy, by writing the two callee bodies out as ordinary local helpers of a throwaway GenServer and running the translator and the walker on them.

Loom.LSP.Supervisor.start_from_config/0 (SAME FILE as Loom.LSP.ConfigListener, so it is in reach of a same-file mechanism): refuses at 'unsupported expression Loom.Config.get(:lsp)', and behind that it calls DynamicSupervisor.start_child/2 once per entry of a config file, inside an Enum.each over data the model does not have. That is a SPAWN of an unknown number of processes, decided by a file on disk. Modelling it as a no-op would say ConfigListener does nothing on :config_loaded, which is false about exactly the thing this model is about; modelling it as a spawn by the caller would put the child under the wrong parent and the wrong link. There is no sound rendering, so it stays blocked.

Loom.Telemetry.Metrics.global_metrics/0 etc. (a DIFFERENT file, so out of reach of a same-file mechanism anyway): refuses at ':ets.lookup(:loom_metrics, :global)'. The model deliberately does not carry ETS contents -- :ets writes are dropped and :ets.new is an opaque fresh reference -- so an ETS READ has no value to return. A constant Term would say the dashboard's assigns never change (false); a fresh Term per read would say two reads never agree (also false). The model would need nondeterminism, and EBehavior is a function.

So the mechanism would have converted one opaque 'call to Mod' blocker into two or three specific ones per module and moved neither module's verdict, at the cost of refactoring local_defs/local_calls_in/reachable_locals/close_locals/rewrite_def_bodies -- the resolution path all thirteen committed Gen files go through. nodes.title: check.sh reported a failing fixture and stayed green
nodes.description: Found by my own two malformed fixtures. The fixtures step was written as a pipeline: run_fixtures.exs piped into grep -v PASS. run_fixtures.exs does System.halt(1) when a fixture fails, but with set -e a pipeline takes its status from the LAST command, and grep succeeded, so check.sh printed two FAIL lines and went on to report every later stage green and exit 0. Fixed by running the suite into a scratch file and checking its status, which keeps the same output shape. The same shape is worth auditing elsewhere in the file: every BEAM driver line is "elixir <driver>.exs | tail -1", so a driver that halts non-zero is swallowed the same way -- but those drivers signal by printing an OK line rather than by exit status, so it is a smaller hole than this one was.

nodes.title: NOTES.md addition for round 8 batch B
nodes.description:
For the translator section, after the LiveView assigns paragraph: A LiveView writes its socket in a pipeline, and a pipeline of assigns is a nest of calls whose innermost argument is the socket variable and whose outer ones are not. The record update the model has takes a variable at its head, because a record state is the flattened constructor and has no whole value to nest one update inside another on. So the chain is unfolded to that variable and folded into one update. That is not an approximation: the intermediate socket of a chain is anonymous, so no value expression in it can name anything but the original, and Elixir evaluates every value of a record update against that same original. The one thing refused is the same key twice in one chain, and only because dropping the discarded write would hide whatever is inside it.

For the findings section: the untyped path had been typing every inferred message payload as the opaque term(). One real module showed that a module with no @type still says something about a payload: it compares it with nil. The model has nil only at an Option, so a payload a clause body nil-tests is term() | nil. The other half of the same fix is a refusal -- comparing anything but an Option with nil is now an error naming the type -- and that refusal is the more important half, because before it the translator emitted (x != none) on an opaque Term, which is Lean that does not elaborate, and the readiness harness (which translates dry and never compiles) counted it as a translated module.

For the approximations section: two real modules in this batch were refused rather than modelled, both at a call into another module. Loom.LSP.Supervisor.start_from_config/0 starts one DynamicSupervisor child per entry of a config file: an unknown number of spawns, decided by data outside the model, under a parent that is not the caller. Loom.Telemetry.Metrics.global_metrics/0 and its siblings read an ETS table, and ETS contents are deliberately not in the model -- a constant would claim the dashboard never changes, a fresh value would claim two reads never agree, and the honest answer is nondeterminism, which a Lean function does not have. Both would need the model to grow, not the translator.

Module 1, BigBillWeb.SearchLive: run the translator and the walker on the original file

BLOCKED, and not by a translator gap. Batch B already took it from distance 2 to distance 1: the only walker blocker left is Search.build_index/0 and the translator dies at 'case scrutinee ... got Search.validate_and_search(query, tab)'. Both are calls into BigBill.Search, a SQLite full-text index. build_index/0 is run for its effect on the index; validate_and_search/2 returns {:ok, results, counts} | {:error, :too_short} and is the case scrutinee of run_search/3. Neither has a sound image in the model: the model has no opaque unknown value (Term is a concrete Nat-backed structure with DecidableEq) and EBehavior has no nondeterministic branch, so a case over an unknown tagged union cannot be expressed. Left blocked.

Module 2, BobsBroadcastWeb.StreamController: generalise raw-process loop detection. The blocker was not 'a receive nested in a body' -- the receive IS the whole body of stream_loop/1; the loop is a defp, and both loop_of/1 in the translator and check_defs/2 in the walker matched only :def.

defp loops land (fixture defp_loop.ex), and with them the state inference comes free: clauses/2 turns receive arms into handle_info clauses with the loop parameter as the state pattern, so state_from_clauses/2 reads term() and 'no @type state and no init/1' disappears for a raw loop. StreamController then reaches its real blocker: chunk(conn, data), i.e. Plug.Conn.chunk/2, which writes bytes onto an HTTP socket. Also in the body: check_backpressure!/0 reads Process.info(self(), :message_queue_len) -- the model HAS a mailbox but EBehavior is not handed it -- and raises on a slow client. Left blocked at chunk/2.
Make the defp generalisation SOUND, not just convenient: a receive loop must be called only in tail position

check_loop_calls/2 + tail_exprs/1 in to_lean.exs. A receive loop models the WHOLE life of a process: its tail says what the process does next and falling out of it is exit(:normal). That is only faithful when every call to the loop is in tail position.  is a blocking receive whose value the caller uses, and the model's only blocking form is GenServer.call, which splits the clause into an await state -- there is nothing here to split. Now an error (fixture error_loop_not_tail.ex) instead of a silently false model.
Multi-argument receive helpers are NOT raw-process loops, and I deliberately did not make them one
nodes.description: Loom.Tools.Shell (collect_output/3), Ensemble.AI.TextGenerator (collect_output/3), Loom.Teams.Debate (do_collect/6) and Loom.Session.Architect (a receive inside a case arm of check_editor_permission/3) all look one generalisation away: allow a loop of arity n and make its state an n-tuple, which the model already has. That would be WRONG for every one of them. Each is a synchronous collect: the caller uses the value the receive block returns (extract_result(buffer), {:error, :timeout}, the accumulated responses, :allowed | :denied). The translator's rule for a loop body that does not tail-call the loop is 'the loop returns, so the process exits :normal' -- which would claim the process dies where in fact the caller goes on. So the arity-1 restriction stays, and the new tail-position check makes explicit what it was standing in for: a receive is a process only when it is the whole life of one.

Of the 55 candidate modules, ZERO have only language-level causes. Every one of the ten closest dies on one of: a call into a sibling application module (BigBill.Search, Loom.LSP.Supervisor, Loom.Telemetry.Metrics, Loom.Teams.CostTracker, Ensemble.Integrations.Deciduous, Runs, Issues, GitHub, SentryClient); a direct :ets read of another process's table; Ecto/Repo/Req/File/Port I/O; or float and DateTime arithmetic. 'Alerts declares no messages' is the right refusal, not a gap. The next real gain is not a translator feature; it is either translating the callee modules too (a whole-application model) or an explicit, declared abstraction for an environment call, which would be an assumption to state, not a translation.

nodes.description: Round 8 landed two LiveViews and both had to say, in the generated file and in the example, that handle_event/3 is a real transition of the real process that the model does not carry. That is now the largest honest gap in the landed set: RadioLive's property (playing is true exactly when now_playing holds a track) is TRUE of the mailbox and FALSE of the running view, because handle_event('play', ..) sets playing on its own. Two ways to close it, neither built: (1) model the browser channel as a second message source -- a LiveView process really does receive its events as messages, so handle_event clauses could become ordinary Msg constructors with the socket as state, which would make the property either provable or a counterexample rather than a caveat; (2) leave it out and state the property as a property of a projection, naming the assigns the browser may write. Option 1 is the one that makes the model bigger in the direction real Phoenix code lives, and it costs the same work handle_call already paid: a second callback kind with its own tag space. Node 729 proposes supervision trees for round 9; this is the smaller and more immediately honest of the two.
